title: In Re: Judge Mark B. Cohen
description: Whether a sitting judge's First Amendment right to free speech protects their partisan commentary and "tout[ing]" of past legislative deeds from disciplinary action under the Code of Judicial Conduct.
plaintiff_argument: Judge Cohen argued that his speech, including partisan commentary and referencing past legislative actions, is protected by his First Amendment rights and does not inherently violate judicial conduct rules.
defendant_argument: The Court of Judicial Discipline/Judicial Conduct Board argued that Judge Cohen's "avidly and insistently partisan tilt" and "tout[ing]" of legislative deeds transgressed the Code of Judicial Conduct, as judges must curtail some free speech rights to maintain impartiality.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the order of the Court of Judicial Discipline, ruling that Judge Mark B. Cohen's partisan commentary and "tout[ing]" of legislative deeds, in context, violated judicial conduct rules, thereby limiting a sitting judge's free speech rights.

title: Commonwealth v. Kurtz
description: Whether there was sufficient evidence of probable cause to support the issuance of the warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that there was sufficient probable cause to support the issuance of the warrant.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that there was insufficient probable cause to support the issuance of the warrant.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of sentence, finding that there was sufficient probable cause to support the warrant.

title: Rivera v. Borough of Pottstown
description: Whether the Borough's Code provisions authorizing administrative warrants for biennial rental inspections on less than individualized probable cause are facially constitutional under Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Borough's Code provisions allowing administrative search warrants for rental inspections without individualized probable cause violate their privacy rights and freedom from unreasonable searches under the Pennsylvania Constitution.
defendant_argument: The Borough's Code provisions are valid, do not violate constitutional rights, and individualized probable cause is not required for administrative warrants for rental inspections.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Borough's Code provisions authorizing administrative warrants for biennial rental inspections on less than individualized probable cause are facially unconstitutional and enjoined the Borough from conducting such inspections.

title: Chilutti v. Uber
description: Whether a trial court order granting a petition to compel arbitration of ongoing litigation constitutes an immediately appealable collateral order, with the plaintiffs arguing it is and the defendants arguing it is not.
plaintiff_argument: The Chiluttis argued that the trial court's order compelling arbitration was an immediately appealable collateral order because postponing review would result in the irreparable loss of their claims, particularly their constitutional right to a jury trial, and that no valid arbitration agreement existed.
defendant_argument: Uber argued that the Superior Court erred by concluding that the trial court's order compelling arbitration met the third prong (irreparability) of the collateral order doctrine, and therefore, the order was not immediately appealable.
decision_outcome: The court held that the trial court's order granting Uber's petition to compel arbitration and staying court proceedings does not qualify as a collateral order, vacated the Superior Court's judgment, and remanded the case with instructions to quash the appeal.

title: Commonwealth v. Hunte
description: Whether Section 3755 of the Vehicle Code, which authorizes warrantless blood draws based on probable cause in certain motor vehicle accident cases, violates the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that Section 3755 is constitutional, asserting that warrantless blood draws are permissible if a warrant is obtained later or if exigent circumstances justify the draw, and that the troopers complied with the law.
defendant_argument: Hunte argued that Section 3755 is unconstitutional because it facially authorizes warrantless blood draws based solely on probable cause, without a warrant or a recognized exception, and that implied consent or exigent circumstances do not justify such a categorical rule.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, declaring Section 3755 of the Vehicle Code unconstitutional under the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, and dismissing related charges.

title: Department of Environmental Protection v. Pennsylvania Legislative Reference Bureau; Bowfin KeyCon Holdings v. Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection
description: Whether environmental nonprofit organizations should be permitted to intervene in litigation concerning the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) Regulation, with the nonprofits arguing for intervention to defend the regulation under environmental rights and the opposing parties arguing against intervention due to adequate representation by the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) and mootness.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (DEP) and the intervening environmental nonprofits argue that the RGGI Regulation is a lawful environmental measure, and the nonprofits have a legally enforceable interest to intervene to defend it, especially under the Environmental Rights Amendment (ERA), as DEP's representation was inadequate.
defendant_argument: The defendants (Pennsylvania Legislative Reference Bureau, Senators, and Representatives) argue that the RGGI Regulation is an unconstitutional tax and exceeds DEP's authority, and that the environmental nonprofits' interests were already adequately represented by DEP, making their intervention unnecessary and the appeal from the preliminary injunction moot.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Commonwealth Court's order denying intervention to the environmental nonprofit organizations, allowing them to participate as parties in the ongoing litigation, and dismissed as moot the appeal from the preliminary injunction due to the issuance of a permanent injunction.

title: Commonwealth v. Anthony Lewis
description: Whether police had reasonable suspicion to pursue Anthony Lewis, leading to the seizure of a firearm, based on his presence in a "high-crime area," proximity to alleged gambling, and flight, thereby justifying the denial of his motion to suppress evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that reasonable suspicion was established by the combination of the area being a high-crime area, Lewis being with a group appearing to gamble, and his flight from police.
defendant_argument: Anthony Lewis argued that he was unlawfully seized when police pursued him without reasonable suspicion, making his abandonment of the firearm coerced and subject to suppression.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, which denied Anthony Lewis's motion to suppress the firearm, finding that reasonable suspicion for the seizure existed.

title: Ferguson v. Department of Transportation
description: Whether using participation in an Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition (ARD) program as a 'prior offense' to suspend a driver's license for a subsequent DUI conviction violates due process under the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Ferguson argues that treating ARD as a 'prior offense' for license suspension is fundamentally unfair and a due process violation because ARD participants are not found guilty and do not admit guilt.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Department of Transportation, Bureau of Driver Licensing, implicitly argues that treating ARD as a 'prior offense' for license suspension is a valid civil sanction rationally related to promoting public safety on roadways.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that treating participation in an ARD program as a 'prior offense' for purposes of a driver's license suspension does not violate the Pennsylvania Constitution.

title: Center for Coalfield Justice v. Washington County Board of Elections
description: Whether county boards of elections must provide notice to electors of defective mail ballots and allow them to cast provisional ballots, and how the Pennsylvania Election Code should be interpreted regarding the processing of mail ballots and provisional ballots.
plaintiff_argument: Electors should be notified of defective mail ballots and allowed to cast provisional ballots, and the court's prior ruling in Genser should apply broadly to all disqualified mail ballots, not just "naked" ones.
defendant_argument: County boards of elections correctly followed the Election Code by recording mail ballot receipt and lacked authority to disqualify ballots or implement "notice and cure" procedures before canvassing, as such procedures are not statutorily required.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that a submitted mail-in ballot packet failing to satisfy mandatory Election Code requirements is a legal nullity, and qualified electors have a statutory right to have their provisional ballots counted if no other ballot can be legally attributed to them, extending this to all disqualified mail ballots and implying a need for "notice and cure" procedures.

title: Firearms Owners Against Crime v. Commissioner of Pennsylvania State Police
description: Whether the Pennsylvania State Police (PSP) is fulfilling its statutory obligation under the Uniform Firearms Act to perform "instantaneous" background checks for firearm purchases and provide "immediate" or "forthwith" responses, and what relief is available for delays.
plaintiff_argument: FOAC argued that PSP is intentionally understaffing the PICS Operations Section, causing delays that violate the Uniform Firearms Act's requirement for "instantaneous" and "immediate" background checks, and that PSP should be compelled to staff adequately and provide refunds for fees when sales are cancelled due to delays.
defendant_argument: PSP argued that "instantaneous" refers to the automated database search, not human intervention, and that "immediate" or "forthwith" allows for a "reasonable time" to complete checks, especially for public safety. PSP also contended that staffing decisions are discretionary, not ministerial, and that the statute does not provide for refunds of background check fees.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of injunctive and mandamus relief and dissolved the preliminary injunction, but reversed the denial of declaratory relief and vacated the denial of leave to amend, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion.

title: In re Prospect Crozer LLC
description: Whether a judicial officer's violation of the Pennsylvania Constitution's Article V, Section 17(a) by holding an incompatible office automatically results in the forfeiture of judicial office and renders their decisions void, or if it creates a conflict of duties that makes their judicial actions voidable.
plaintiff_argument: Prospect argued that Judge Braxton held incompatible offices in violation of Article V, Section 17(a), leading to the automatic forfeiture of his judicial office and rendering his orders legal nullities due to structural error.
defendant_argument: The District argued that the Commonwealth Court lacked authority to determine a Section 17(a) violation, that only the Judicial Conduct Board and Court of Judicial Discipline could, and that even if a violation occurred, it did not result in automatic forfeiture of judicial office.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order to vacate the trial court's orders and remand the cases for reassignment to a new judge, concluding that Judge Braxton's actions created a constitutionally impermissible conflict of duties, making his judicial actions voidable.

title: Crawford v. Commonwealth
description: Whether state firearm preemption laws (FPLs) violate the Pennsylvania Constitution by infringing on the right to life and liberty, creating a state-created danger, or improperly interfering with delegated public health duties of local municipalities, thereby preventing local governments from enacting gun control measures.
plaintiff_argument: Appellants argue that state firearm preemption laws (FPLs) violate their substantive due process rights under Article I, Section 1 of the Pennsylvania Constitution by depriving them of the right to enjoy and defend life and liberty, create a state-created danger by preventing local gun safety measures, and improperly interfere with Philadelphia's delegated public health responsibilities.
defendant_argument: Appellees contend that the FPLs are constitutional, within the General Assembly's legislative power, do not violate substantive due process as there is no collective right to self-defense by local legislation, and do not create a state-created danger. They also argue that the LHAL and DPCL do not delegate authority to regulate firearms to local entities.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order dismissing the Petition with prejudice, ruling against the appellants' challenges to the state firearm preemption laws.

title: In re The Thirtieth County Investigating Grand Jury
description: Whether an investigating grand jury report met the statutory definition for public release and whether all named, non-indicted individuals criticized in such a report are entitled to due process notice and an opportunity to be heard.
plaintiff_argument: The Petitioner argued that the grand jury report did not meet the statutory definition for public release and that all named, non-indicted individuals criticized in the report are entitled to due process notice and an opportunity to be heard.
defendant_argument: The DAO argued that the grand jury report satisfied the statutory definition for public release and that the supervising judge had discretion in providing notice and opportunity to respond to criticized individuals.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the supervising judge's order to unseal the report, ruling that the report did not meet the statutory definition for public release, and remanded with instructions to permanently seal it, further determining that all named but nonindicted individuals criticized in a grand jury report must be given notice and an opportunity to respond.

title: Genser v. Butler County Board of Elections
description: Whether a provisional ballot should be counted when a voter's initial mail-in ballot was timely received but deemed void due to the absence of a secrecy envelope, with plaintiffs arguing for counting to prevent disenfranchisement and defendants arguing against it, asserting that a timely received mail-in ballot, even if defective, precludes a provisional ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The Electors and the Pennsylvania Democratic Party (PDP) argued that a mail-in ballot lacking a Secrecy Envelope is void and therefore does not constitute a 'ballot cast' or 'voted' in a manner that should prevent the counting of a subsequent provisional ballot, emphasizing the need to interpret election laws to enfranchise voters and prevent disenfranchisement.
defendant_argument: The Republican National Committee and Republican Party (Appellants) argued that the General Assembly alone sets election rules, and a timely received mail-in ballot, even if defective, should preclude counting a provisional ballot, viewing such an action as an unauthorized 'curing' procedure contrary to the Election Code's plain language.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, ruling that the Butler County Board of Elections erred in refusing to count the Electors' provisional ballots, as their initial mail-in ballots were void and thus did not prevent the counting of a valid provisional ballot.

title: Commonwealth v. Yard
description: Whether the evidentiary limitation of "proof is evident or presumption great" applies to the life-offense exception to the right to bail under the Pennsylvania Constitution, or only to the dangerousness exception.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the "proof is evident or presumption great" standard from Commonwealth v. Talley does not apply to the life-imprisonment exception, meaning bail should be denied for first-degree murder charges.
defendant_argument: Michael Noel Yard argued that the Talley standard (proof is evident or presumption great) does apply to the life-imprisonment exception, and the Commonwealth failed to meet this standard with a "cold record," thus he should be granted bail.
decision_outcome: The court held that the proof/presumption limitation does not apply to the life-offense exception to the right to bail, meaning bail is categorically precluded for offenses with a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. The lower court's order granting nominal bail was vacated.

title: Krasner v. Ward
description: Whether Articles of Impeachment passed by one session of the General Assembly carry over into a subsequent legislative assembly after the previous session adjourned sine die, with the plaintiff arguing they do not and the defendant arguing they do.
plaintiff_argument: The Articles of Impeachment, as pending business, became null and void upon the sine die adjournment of the 206th General Assembly on November 30, 2022, and therefore cannot carry over to the 207th General Assembly.
defendant_argument: The Articles of Impeachment and related legislative business are not terminated by the sine die adjournment of a General Assembly session and can carry over to a new session, as impeachment is a judicial power distinct from legislative functions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's decision, holding that the Articles of Impeachment passed by the 206th Session of the General Assembly became null and void upon its expiration on November 30, 2022.

title: Oberholzer v. Galapo
description: Whether signs decrying hatred and racism, placed by a Jewish family on their own lawn after a neighbor called one of them a "fucking Jew," were properly enjoined by the trial court.
plaintiff_argument: The Oberholzers argued that the signs constituted targeted picketing, created a false light, were defamatory, invaded their privacy, and caused emotional distress, thus warranting an injunction to prevent irreparable harm and protect their constitutional right to quiet enjoyment of their property.
defendant_argument: The Galapos argued that their signs constituted pure speech protected by Article I, Section 7 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, and that the injunction was an impermissible prior restraint on their free speech, regardless of any tort claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania affirmed the Superior Court's decision to vacate the injunction against the Galapos' signs, ordering the injunction dissolved.

title: Commonwealth v. Thompson
description: Whether inventory searches remain valid under Pennsylvania's Constitution following the rejection of the federal automobile exception to the warrant requirement.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that inventory searches are invalid under Pennsylvania's Constitution, especially after the rejection of the federal automobile exception.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that inventory searches remain valid under Pennsylvania's Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the appeal as having been improvidently granted.

title: Commonwealth v. Torsilieri
description: Whether the General Assembly's determination that individuals who commit sexual offenses pose a high risk of committing additional sexual offenses constitutes an unconstitutional irrebuttable presumption violative of due process and the right to reputation, and whether the registration and notification requirements in Subchapter H of SORNA constitute criminal punishment.
plaintiff_argument: Appellee argued that SORNA's irrebuttable presumption is unconstitutional because it is not universally true and impairs the right to reputation. He also contended that SORNA's registration and notification requirements constitute criminal punishment, violating separation of powers, cruel and unusual punishment, and the right to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth argued that Appellee failed to demonstrate a scientific consensus that SORNA's presumption is false. It maintained that SORNA's purpose is public protection through information sharing, not punishment or recidivism reduction, and that its requirements are not excessive or punitive.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's order, finding that Appellee failed to prove SORNA's irrebuttable presumption was unconstitutional and that Subchapter H's registration and notification requirements do not constitute criminal punishment.

title: City of Lancaster v. Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission
description: Whether Section 59.18 of the PUC's regulations, which grants discretion to natural gas distribution companies for gas meter placement in historic districts, constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The Municipalities argued that Section 59.18 unlawfully delegates unfettered legislative authority to natural gas distribution companies without adequate standards, violating the Pennsylvania Constitution.
defendant_argument: The PUC contended that Section 59.18 is a regulatory act for public safety, not an unconstitutional delegation, as the General Assembly never vested the PUC with legislative authority over meter locations in historic districts.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's order, concluding that the General Assembly never enacted a statute vesting the PUC with legislative authority over gas meter locations in historic districts, thus no unconstitutional delegation occurred.

title: Scott v. Pennsylvania Board of Parole
description: Whether the Commonwealth Court has original jurisdiction to hear claims challenging the constitutionality of a statute that renders individuals sentenced to life imprisonment ineligible for parole, or if such claims are in the nature of post-conviction relief and thus outside its jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Commonwealth Court had original jurisdiction because they were not challenging their life imprisonment sentences but rather their parole eligibility, which they contended was a separate matter, and that depriving them of parole opportunities violated state and federal constitutions.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Commonwealth Court lacked jurisdiction because the plaintiffs' claims were in the nature of applications for post-conviction relief, which is statutorily excluded from the Commonwealth Court's original jurisdiction, and that parole eligibility is integral to the criminal sentence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's holding that it lacked jurisdiction over the appellants' petition, concluding that the claims fundamentally challenged the constitutionality of their sentences and thus fell under post-conviction relief.

title: Siger v. City of Chester
description: Whether the Receiver's proposed modifications to the City of Chester's recovery plan are lawful and within the Receiver's statutory authority under Act 47, with the City arguing they unlawfully deprive elected officials of their authority and alter the form of government, and the Receiver arguing they are necessary for financial stability.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Receiver) argued that the proposed modifications to the recovery plan were necessary to achieve financial stability for the distressed municipality and were within the statutory authority granted by Act 47, which supersedes the City's Home Rule Charter.
defendant_argument: The defendant (City of Chester) argued that the Receiver's proposed modifications were unlawful, exceeded the Receiver's statutory authority, impermissibly altered the City's form of government, and infringed upon the powers of its elected officials.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the order of the Commonwealth Court, upholding the Receiver's proposed modifications to the City of Chester's recovery plan.

title: Weeks v. Department of Human Service of the Commonwealth
description: Whether Act 12 of 2019 was enacted in violation of Article III, Sections 1 and 3 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, with the plaintiffs arguing it violated original purpose and single subject rules, and the defendant arguing it satisfied all constitutional requirements.
plaintiff_argument: Appellants argued that Act 12 violated Article III, Sections 1 and 3, because its original purpose changed, its title was deceptive, and its provisions covered more than a single subject, leading to unconstitutional logrolling.
defendant_argument: DHS argued that Act 12 satisfied Article III requirements, as its original purpose (broadly defined as providing medical assistance to low-income individuals) did not change, its title was not deceptive, and all provisions were germane to a single unifying subject.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, holding that the legislative process for Act 12 satisfied the constitutional requirements of Article III, Sections 1 and 3, and thus the statutory enactment is constitutional.

title: The Marcellus Shale Coalition v. Department of Environmental Protection of the Commonwealth
description: Whether the Department of Environmental Protection and the Environmental Quality Board exceeded their legislative rulemaking authority under the Pennsylvania Oil and Gas Act of 1984 by defining "other critical communities," "common areas of a school's property," "playgrounds," and including "playground owners" as "public resource agencies" in their regulations for unconventional gas wells.
plaintiff_argument: The Agencies exceeded their statutory authority by promulgating new definitions for "public resources" and "public resource agencies" that substantially alter the well permit application process and are not expressly authorized by Act 13, and that the PNDI database incorporation violates the Documents Law.
defendant_argument: The General Assembly conferred broad legislative rulemaking powers, and the challenged regulations are a reasonable exercise of that authority, consistent with the purposes of the Oil and Gas Act and the Environmental Rights Amendment, and the PNDI process was properly promulgated.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's order, finding that the Department of Environmental Protection and the Environmental Quality Board did not exceed their legislative rulemaking powers in enacting the challenged regulations.

title: GM Berkshire Hills LLC v. Berks County Board of Assessment
description: Whether a school district's method of selectively appealing property assessments, based on recent sales, a common level ratio, and a cost-benefit threshold, violates the Uniformity Clause of the Pennsylvania Constitution by creating discriminatory results.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues the school district's selective assessment appeal method is discriminatory and violates the Uniformity Clause, leading to an unfair tax burden because it targets outliers and creates a prohibited subclass.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues their property selection method for assessment appeals is neutral, enhances uniformity by equalizing assessment ratios, and does not create a prohibited subclass.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's decision, finding the school district's property assessment appeal method violated the Uniformity Clause.

title: McLinko v. Commonwealth
description: Whether the General Assembly overstepped its power and violated the Pennsylvania Constitution when it enacted legislation allowing for universal mail-in voting.
plaintiff_argument: The Pennsylvania Constitution requires in-person voting, with narrow exceptions for absentee voters, and Act 77's universal mail-in voting provisions are unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The General Assembly has the constitutional authority to enact legislation allowing for universal mail-in voting, and Act 77 is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's order, finding Act 77's universal mail-in voting provisions constitutional.

title: Pennsylvania Environmental Defense Foundation v. Commonwealth
description: Whether the Commonwealth's use of funds derived from oil and gas leases on state lands, and related legislative changes, violate the Environmental Rights Amendment by not solely serving trust purposes.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth's use of oil and gas lease proceeds for DCNR's general operations, allocation to projects outside the Marcellus Shale region, the repeal of the Oil and Gas Lease Fund Act, transfer of control to the General Assembly, commingling of funds, and transfer of Keystone Fund monies to the General Fund violate the Environmental Rights Amendment and the Commonwealth's trustee duties.
defendant_argument: The challenged uses of funds and legislative changes are consistent with the Environmental Rights Amendment and the Commonwealth's trustee duties, as DCNR's operations are necessary for conservation, there are no geographic restrictions on fund use, the Lease Fund remains a special fund with explicit trustee duty considerations, separate accounts are not mandated, and the Keystone Fund does not involve trust assets.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, concluding that PEDF failed to demonstrate that the challenged provisions violate the Pennsylvania Constitution, thereby ruling against PEDF on all its claims.

title: Commonwealth v. Jones-Williams
description: Whether the warrantless seizure of a DUI suspect's blood, drawn by hospital personnel and later requested by police without a warrant, was lawful under the exigent circumstances exception or the implied consent statute (75 Pa.C.S. § 3755).
plaintiff_argument: The warrantless seizure of blood was lawful under the exigent circumstances exception, as the defendant was unconscious and required medical treatment, and also permissible under the implied consent statute (Section 3755) because police had probable cause and complied with the statute.
defendant_argument: The blood seizure was illegal because there were no exigent circumstances as the blood was already drawn and preserved, and the implied consent statute (Section 3755) is unconstitutional and cannot bypass the warrant requirement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Superior Court's decision to suppress the blood test results and remand for a new trial, finding that no exigent circumstances justified the warrantless seizure of the defendant's blood. The Court vacated the Superior Court's ruling on the unconstitutionality of Section 3755, deeming it unnecessary to address.

title: Khalil v. Williams
description: Whether legal malpractice claims against attorneys following a settlement are barred by the Muhammad rule, or if exceptions apply when the claims are based on incorrect legal advice rather than the settlement amount, or on fraud.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that her legal malpractice claims were not barred by the Muhammad rule because they were based on her attorneys' erroneous legal advice regarding the scope and effect of a settlement release, which precluded her counterclaims in a separate case, and not merely on dissatisfaction with the settlement amount. She also alleged fraud, claiming the release she signed was switched.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiff's claims were barred by the Muhammad rule because her true objective was to revisit the settlement amount, and her fraud allegations had been previously rejected. They contended the case was distinguishable from precedents that allowed claims based on incorrect advice on well-established principles of law.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed in part and affirmed in part the Superior Court's decision, holding that certain of the plaintiff's claims (negligence and breach of contract based on incorrect legal advice) are not barred by Muhammad, and her fraud claim can proceed, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Commonwealth v. Edwards
description: Whether a prosecutor's intentional racial discrimination during jury selection, in violation of Batson v. Kentucky, constitutes prosecutorial overreaching sufficient to preclude retrial on double jeopardy grounds under the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Derrick Edwards, argued that the prosecutor's intentional racial discrimination in jury selection (a Batson violation) was egregious prosecutorial misconduct that deprived him of a fair trial and subverted the truth-determining process, thus barring retrial under double jeopardy principles.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, argued that while a Batson violation warrants a new trial, it does not constitute the 'overwhelming and egregious' misconduct or 'deliberate, bad faith' intent required to preclude retrial on double jeopardy grounds, especially since the prosecutor's actions were not intended to provoke a mistrial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Superior Court, which affirmed the trial court's order denying the Appellant's motion to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds, thereby allowing retrial.

title: Commonwealth v. Barr
description: Whether the smell of marijuana alone can establish probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search, given the legalization of medical marijuana.
plaintiff_argument: The smell of marijuana alone should not establish probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search because medical marijuana is legal, and the Hicks decision dictates that lawful possession of an item cannot alone suggest criminal activity.
defendant_argument: The smell of marijuana remains a relevant factor for probable cause in a warrantless vehicle search, as the Medical Marijuana Act (MMA) only provides a limited exception to the general illegality of marijuana, and Hicks is distinguishable.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Superior Court's judgment, reinstated the trial court's order granting the Appellant's motion to suppress, and remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion, ruling that the odor of marijuana alone does not amount to probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search.

title: In re Interest of Y.W.-B.
description: Whether a child protective services agency can compel a home inspection based on an anonymous report without establishing sufficient probable cause, thereby violating Fourth Amendment and state constitutional protections against unreasonable searches, with the plaintiff arguing against such authority and the defendant arguing for a less stringent probable cause standard.
plaintiff_argument: Mother argued that the Superior Court's decision created an unconstitutionally diluted version of the probable cause standard, violating her rights under the Fourth Amendment and Article 1, Section 8, by eliminating requirements for particularity, reliability of the source, and a nexus between allegations and the home.
defendant_argument: DHS agreed that probable cause must be established but rejected strict enforcement of criminal law probable cause standards, arguing that a less stringent standard applies to child protective services investigations and that particularity and nexus requirements are not strictly necessary for neglect investigations.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court concluded that the Department of Human Services (DHS) did not establish sufficient probable cause to compel a home inspection and therefore reversed the order of the Superior Court.

title: Commonwealth v. Talley
description: Whether the Commonwealth must provide clear and convincing evidence to deny bail based on public safety, and whether text message screenshots omitting metadata are admissible under the Best Evidence Rule.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the standard of proof for denying bail based on public safety is a 'prima facie case' and that text message screenshots, even without metadata, are admissible as originals or duplicates under the best-evidence rule.
defendant_argument: Talley argued that denying bail requires 'clear and convincing evidence' and that the Commonwealth failed to meet this burden. He also contended that text message screenshots omitting metadata violate the best-evidence rule and are inadmissible.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, upholding Talley's conviction and sentence, finding that while the trial court erred in denying bail, the error was harmless and did not affect the trial outcome, and that the text message screenshots were admissible.

title: League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania v. Degraffenreid
description: Whether the proposed Victim's Rights Amendment, presented as a single ballot question, violated Article XI, Section 1 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, which requires that multiple amendments be voted upon separately.
plaintiff_argument: The proposed Victim's Rights Amendment violates the separate vote requirement of Article XI, Section 1 because it contains multiple, distinct, and non-interrelated changes that substantively affect various existing constitutional provisions, thereby denying voters the right to approve or disapprove each change individually.
defendant_argument: The Victim's Rights Amendment is sufficiently interrelated and serves the common purpose of enshrining victims' rights, and it does not explicitly alter the language of other constitutional provisions, thus complying with the "separate vote" requirement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, declaring the proposed Victim's Rights Amendment unconstitutional for violating the separate vote requirement and permanently enjoining the Secretary of the Commonwealth from tabulating or certifying the election results.

title: Brooks v. Ewing Cole, Inc.
description: Whether an order denying a summary judgment motion based on sovereign immunity is an appealable collateral order under Pennsylvania Rule of Appellate Procedure 313.
plaintiff_argument: The order denying summary judgment is not a collateral order because sovereign immunity can be reexamined after final judgment, and the Family Court's delay in raising the defense indicates it is not a critical issue for immediate appeal.
defendant_argument: The order denying summary judgment is a collateral order because sovereign immunity is an absolute immunity from suit, and this protection is irreparably lost if the government is forced to litigate before an appeal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's decision, concluding that an order denying summary judgment on sovereign immunity grounds is a collateral order appealable as of right, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Pennsylvania Environmental Defense Foundation v. Commonwealth
description: Whether revenues from oil and gas leases on state lands, specifically bonus payments, rental fees, and interest penalties, constitute trust assets that must be returned to the trust corpus or if they are income that can be diverted to the General Fund.
plaintiff_argument: The PEDF argued that all revenues (bonus, rental, interest penalties) are inextricably linked to the sale of trust assets and must be returned to the trust corpus as principal, and that the ERA does not create income entitlements for beneficiaries.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth argued that bonus and rent payments are for an inchoate leasehold interest, not the sale of minerals, and thus are income that can be diverted, aligning with the 1947 Act's provisions for income distribution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court, holding that while bonus payments, rentals, and late fees are income, the Environmental Rights Amendment (ERA) does not create income entitlements for beneficiaries, and therefore these revenues must be returned to the trust corpus for conservation and maintenance.

title: Commonwealth v. Eid
description: Whether the sentencing provision in 75 Pa.C.S. § 1543(b)(1.1)(i) is unconstitutionally vague because it fails to provide a clear statutory maximum penalty for refusing chemical testing after driving under a suspended license, violating state and federal due process principles.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the DUS statute is not unconstitutionally vague and a maximum term of six months can be reasonably inferred by reading it in conjunction with other sections of the Vehicle Code and historical legislative intent.
defendant_argument: Khalid Eid argued that the sentencing statute is unconstitutionally vague because it lacks an express maximum penalty, thereby violating due process by failing to provide fair notice of the consequences of one's actions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Eid's conviction for refusing chemical testing but vacated his sentence of imprisonment, ruling that the sentencing statute was unconstitutionally vague due to the absence of a specified maximum term, and affirmed the mandatory $1,000 fine.

title: Commonwealth v. Hairston
description: Whether the death penalty is unconstitutional under the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I, Section 13 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, and whether trial and appellate counsel provided ineffective assistance.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the death penalty is constitutional, the verdict slip was valid, the prosecutor's arguments were proper, and that counsel was effective in all challenged aspects.
defendant_argument: Hairston argued that the death penalty is unconstitutional both facially and as-applied, and that his trial and appellate counsel were ineffective for failing to challenge the verdict slip, allowing prosecutorial misconduct, and allowing improper expert testimony.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the PCRA court's order denying relief, upholding Kenneth Hairston's death sentence and rejecting his claims of unconstitutionality and ineffective assistance of counsel.

title: Commonwealth v. Middaugh
description: Whether a lengthy delay by a court clerk in notifying PennDOT of a DUI conviction, leading to a delayed license suspension, violates a driver's due process rights and should preclude the suspension.
plaintiff_argument: PennDOT argued that it cannot suspend a license until it receives official notification, and since the delay was caused by the court clerk, not PennDOT, the suspension should be upheld.
defendant_argument: Stephen Middaugh argued that the lengthy delay in notifying him of the suspension, regardless of who caused it, resulted in significant prejudice due to changes in his life circumstances and medical needs, thus violating his due process rights.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, which had rescinded Stephen Middaugh's driving privilege suspension.
